Ephesians 4
ee-FEE-zhuhnz FOR
proper noun
The fourth chapter of Paul’s epistle to the Ephesians; the hinge from the doctrine of chapters 1–3 to the walk of chapters 4–6.

📖 Biblical Definition

Ephesians 4 is the great turning of Paul’s epistle from doctrine to duty, where the apostle, having set forth the riches of grace and the eternal purpose of God in the first three chapters, beseeches the saints to walk worthy of the calling wherewith they are called. The chapter opens with the unity of the Spirit, grounded in seven ones—one body, one Spirit, one hope, one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all—a unity the church does not create but keeps in the bond of peace. Then the ascended Christ is shown giving gifts to His church: apostles, prophets, evangelists, and pastors and teachers, given for the perfecting of the saints, for the work of the ministry, and for the edifying of the body, that the church may grow up into the Head, into Christ, no more tossed about by every wind of doctrine. The chapter closes with the new walk: putting off the old man, corrupt according to the deceitful lusts, and putting on the new man, created after God in righteousness and true holiness—speaking truth, laboring honestly, grieving not the Holy Spirit, and forgiving as God in Christ has forgiven. The dictionary reads Ephesians 4 as the pattern of the church’s unity, ministry, and sanctification: doctrine first, then the walk that flows from it.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

The fourth chapter of Ephesians; the unity of the Spirit, the ascended Christ’s gifts to His church, and the putting off of the old man and putting on of the new.

⚠️ Modern Corruption

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition, though the chapter’s gifts are misread to support continuing apostles, and its unity is invoked to flatten doctrinal difference.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Two misreadings touch the chapter. The first takes the gift of apostles and prophets as offices continuing in the church today, the proof-text of the New Apostolic Reformation; but the apostles and prophets are named the foundation of the church (Eph 2:20), and a foundation is laid once—the dictionary holds the cessation of these founding offices with the close of the canon. The second invokes the unity of the Spirit to flatten real doctrinal difference, as though peace were purchased by silence on the truth; but the same chapter sets the goal as growing up into the Head and no more being tossed by every wind of doctrine. True unity is unity in the truth.

The principle to recover is the chapter’s own order: the unity the church keeps is grounded in the seven ones and aims at maturity in sound doctrine; the gifts are given to edify the body until it grows up into Christ; and the new walk flows from the new man created in righteousness and true holiness. Doctrine produces duty; the worthy walk is the fruit of the grace set forth in the chapters before.
